 nodes to their patches are always very sparse. So really
 hard to tell how exploitable these memory corruptions are
 and whether they actually will lead to code execution. Also,
 we got at least one memory corruption in WebKit that of
 course affects Safari and anything sort of exposed via a
 website that a user may visit. There's also, as usual for
 Apple, a separate Safari update. The reason you have
 this is because some of the older operating systems, well,
 they may now need a newer version of Safari to address
 the WebKit issues that Apple patched because they
 originally came with an older version of Safari. But for the
 current operating systems, you shouldn't really see a
 separate Safari update. Xcode also was updated, and that's
 also whenever they update the operating system. Of course,
 Xcode, which is Apple's development environment, well,
 has to be updated as well. So overall, nothing terribly
 exciting, nothing that's already being exploited, but
 certainly patches that you probably want to apply
 sometime this week if possible. Well, I've got an
 interesting blog post by Proofpoint showing how cyber
 criminals are targeting trucking and logistic. So
 what's happening here is that these criminals, their end
 goal is to steal trucks or to load being transported by
 those trucks. But in order to do so, they need to know which
 trucks actually has load worth stealing. A lot of times, it
 sort of happens randomly, where basically just parked
 trailers and such are being stolen with whatever load they
 have. But for cyber criminals, of course, much better to then
 being able to figure out which truck actually has a high
 value load. The way this particular scheme works is
 that they initially compromise one company, one trucking or
 logistics company, just via standard fake emails and
 phishing. And once they take control of one company,
 they're using legitimate remote managing and monitoring
 tools like your standard log me in and things like that, in
 order to then basically see what they're working on. But
 they're also using that initial access to then infect
 other trucking companies by, for example, posting fake
 loads and fake offers for work on various systems that these
 trucking companies use. And those fake offers are then
 often being used to trick a victim into clicking on
 malicious links and downloading, installing
 malicious malware just by, for example, posting PDFs and the
 likes. So basically, standard phishing tricks. But by being
 inside these systems, it's, of course, a lot more convincing
 than to get a user to execute or open an attachment. The end
 goal, as I said, is just to figure out which truck has a
 particular value below it and then steal it. And apparently
 the losses for these particular schemes are ranging
 in the billions at this point. From a defensive point of
 view, well, you always need to control these remote
 management tools. That's probably, I think, the biggest
 lesson here from this particular compromise. They're
 often used as ransomware attacks and other attacks
 where an attacker, in order to gain persistent access to a
 system, just installs a legitimate remote management
 tool instead of an obvious malicious one, which, of
 course, is much easier to detect by anti-malware
 endpoint protection systems. And we don't just have patches
 from Apple. Google also released its usual scheduled
 monthly update. This is the November 2025 update that they
 published for Android. The vulnerability is actually kind
 of so similar in scope to what I just talked about when it
 came to Apple. So we have a couple of vulnerabilities here
 that sort of could lead to these single click or no click
 exploits, where just viewing an image or something like
 this will lead to a system compromise. For example, we
 have here one vulnerability in what Google refers to as
 system. So basically, the basic operating system that
 does allow remote code execution and is assigned a
 severity of critical affecting Android back to version 13. A
 little bit more detail here from Google than we do get
 from Apple with this severity and also the type actually
 indicating that remote code execution is possible here
 with this particular vulnerability. As usual, apply
 these Android patches as as they become available for your
 particular device. Of course, there may be a delay depending
 on your carrier and what device you are using. Well,
 and that's it for today. So thanks for listening and
 special thanks to anybody who is recommending this podcast
 on Apple's podcast site and also leaving a comment there.
 And that's it for today and talk to you again tomorrow.
 Bye.

episodes.transcript: 00:00.433 --> 00:02.702 Hey, it’s Jack, host of the show. 00:02.702 --> 00:05.972 For a while, I worked at a big company doing security engineering, 00:06.373 --> 00:09.275 and every year, someone would come in and do an audit on us, 00:09.275 --> 00:13.580 and they would ask us the same question; do you have a security policy? 00:13.980 --> 00:15.448 Yes, of course we do. 00:15.448 --> 00:18.618 Is it available for all your employees to find? 00:19.052 --> 00:21.988 Yep. It’s right there on SharePoint. 00:21.988 --> 00:25.458 But this got me thinking — yeah, sure, it was right there in SharePoint, 00:25.825 --> 00:31.264 but it was called something ridiculous like isp_overview or something like that. 00:31.798 --> 00:34.801 ISP stood for information security policy. 00:35.101 --> 00:38.938 It made me wonder; if this document was so important that we would be audited 00:39.205 --> 00:43.209 to check to see if we had it and make sure all our employees had access to it, 00:43.743 --> 00:46.746 could any of them actually find it if they needed it? 00:47.547 --> 00:50.450 This policy said stuff like what are our security objectives? 00:50.450 --> 00:51.985 Who are the people that we escalate things 00:51.985 --> 00:54.988 to? What’s acceptable in our network and not? 00:55.021 --> 00:56.890 Who should be able to access what, 00:56.890 --> 00:58.958 as well as what we should do when there’s an incident, 00:58.958 --> 01:02.062 how often our security training should be, and what our security standards are. 01:02.595 --> 01:07.801 So, one day when I was feeling feisty, I decided to do something to make a point. 01:08.201 --> 01:11.204 I asked everyone on shift in our network operations center — hey, 01:11.337 --> 01:14.941 you have fifteen minutes to find the company’s security policy. 01:15.308 --> 01:18.912 Winner gets a free item in the vending machine. Go. 01:18.912 --> 01:19.779 Everyone started looking. 01:19.779 --> 01:22.949 First they typed ‘security policy’ in our department’s portal. 01:23.616 --> 01:26.252 That actually brought up security policies for some of our customers, 01:26.252 --> 01:27.987 which I thought was really cool that our customers 01:27.987 --> 01:30.890 were taking their security policy so seriously that they wanted to make sure 01:30.890 --> 01:34.461 that their partners had copies of it. But that wasn’t our policy. 01:34.861 --> 01:36.563 Then people started looking through their e-mails. 01:36.563 --> 01:39.566 Nope, nothing in our e-mail about security policy. 01:39.933 --> 01:41.568 Then they looked at shared drives. 01:41.568 --> 01:42.936 They couldn't find anything there, 01:42.936 --> 01:45.939 and eventually a few of them thought to look through SharePoint. 01:45.972 --> 01:49.342 Of course, not a single one of them could find it 01:49.542 --> 01:52.912 because it had the worst name and it was in the worst place. 01:53.379 --> 01:56.816 I don't know if you've ever used SharePoint, but it’s a place to store 01:56.816 --> 02:00.386 documentation and files, and it’s an awful mess to navigate and find stuff. 02:00.553 --> 02:03.556 None of their searches came close to finding it. 02:03.623 --> 02:05.492 So, I just said, alright everyone, time’s up. 02:05.492 --> 02:07.327 Thanks for trying. 02:07.327 --> 02:11.297 Then I sent an e-mail to our CISO, our Chief Information Security Officer. 02:11.297 --> 02:13.600 Security policy test queue one: 02:13.600 --> 02:16.469 Ten out of ten of our NOC technicians could not find our company’s 02:16.469 --> 02:18.872 security policy after spending fifteen minutes trying. 02:20.006 --> 02:23.443 He responded, um, sounds like your NOC technicians 02:23.443 --> 02:25.545 have a hard time finding things? 02:25.545 --> 02:27.247 I waited another four months. 02:27.247 --> 02:30.450 We got a whole new batch of technicians, and I try it again. 02:30.717 --> 02:32.952 One guy actually found it. I was really impressed. 02:32.952 --> 02:35.955 I also re-tested all the people that I tested four months ago. 02:36.022 --> 02:38.791 One in five remembered where I told them it was. 02:38.791 --> 02:40.160 So, I sent another e-mail. 02:40.160 --> 02:43.163 Nine out of ten of our new hires could not find our security policy. 02:43.196 --> 02:46.199 Four out of five of our senior technicians could not find it. 02:46.833 --> 02:48.902 He was like, why do you keep telling me this? 02:48.902 --> 02:51.137 Just show them where it is. 02:51.137 --> 02:55.308 I wanted him to understand the problem wasn’t my technicians. 02:55.308 --> 02:59.312 It was that the security policy was buried way too deep. 02:59.445 --> 03:02.081 It was named poorly, and nobody knew where it was. 03:02.081 --> 03:05.084 Nobody could find it if they tried, which meant nobody knew what was in it. 03:05.552 --> 03:09.422 In my opinion, when there’s a document that’s so important that auditors ask 03:09.422 --> 03:12.425 if you have it and if it’s available for employees to find, 03:12.759 --> 03:14.794 then it should be way more front and center. 03:14.794 --> 03:18.798 Heck, I even suggested that we should print out a summary of it 03:18.798 --> 03:22.202 and tape it above the urinals and sinks in the bathroom 03:22.468 --> 03:25.171 so that everyone sees it every time they go to the bathroom. 03:25.171 --> 03:26.873 That way the whole company would be familiar 03:26.873 --> 03:28.775 with our security policy and know exactly what to do 03:28.775 --> 03:31.177 when there’s an incident and what’s allowed and not allowed. 03:31.177 --> 03:36.149 But of course, our security leadership didn’t see it that way and never did 03:36.149 --> 03:41.988 change the name of it or the location, and we kept passing our audits somehow. 03:42.889 --> 03:46.759 Yet, nobody in the company ever read it or knew where it was. 03:46.759 --> 03:51.664 Ah, the politics of office life and compliance. [INTRO MUSIC] 03:56.502 --> 03:58.037 These are true stories from 03:58.037 --> 04:01.040 the dark side of the internet. 04:03.343 --> 04:05.912 I’m Jack Rhysider. 04:05.912 --> 04:08.915 This is Darknet Diaries. 04:22.295 --> 04:24.063 [INTRO MUSIC ENDS] Today I have the pleasure of sitting down 04:24.063 --> 04:27.734 and hearing stories from Tanya Janca. Thank you for having me. I’ve been going 04:27.734 --> 04:31.904 to a lot of conferences, and time and time again I see Tanya at almost all of them. 04:32.105 --> 04:34.974 But not only is she there, but she’s almost always giving talks 04:34.974 --> 04:35.875 when she’s there. 04:35.875 --> 04:38.845 She’s on a mission and is very driven. 04:38.845 --> 04:42.949 I hope software developers write more secure code. 04:42.949 --> 04:46.919 Boiled down to a word, that’s called appsec, application security. 04:47.120 --> 04:51.257 She’s laser-focused on how applications become insecure 04:51.457 --> 04:53.092 and how to make them secure. 04:53.092 --> 04:56.462 I was a software developer forever, and then someone exploited 04:56.462 --> 05:00.366 one of my apps and showed me, and it created this fascination. 05:00.833 --> 05:04.704 It was an SQL injection and it was on the log-in screen 05:04.704 --> 05:08.041 of one of my team’s apps, and I was in charge of the team. 05:08.508 --> 05:10.576 So, if it’s not secure, it’s my fault. 05:12.478 --> 05:13.446 I remember he was giving a 05:13.446 --> 05:18.017 demonstration to us, and he showed me — he’s like, this is one of your apps. 05:18.017 --> 05:21.354 I’m gonna get past this log-in screen without a password, 05:21.621 --> 05:24.457 and the only reason it’s gonna take so long is because 05:24.457 --> 05:27.460 I’m talking, and it’s gonna be a minute. [Music] 05:28.027 --> 05:30.396 He demonstrated how he can easily get past her 05:30.396 --> 05:33.399 log-in screen, and showed her how it was done. 05:33.399 --> 05:36.502 She was stunned. Like, oh my god. 05:36.502 --> 05:40.973 This was the moment that she saw the whole world differently. 05:41.140 --> 05:45.111 Just because there’s a right way to use a website by putting in a username 05:45.111 --> 05:48.214 where it says ‘username’ and a password where it says ‘password’ doesn't 05:48.214 --> 05:51.517 mean people actually play by those rules and follow the website’s logic. 05:51.951 --> 05:54.787 If you're clever enough to think outside the box, 05:54.787 --> 05:57.790 you can manipulate the website to do things 05:57.890 --> 06:02.095 that the developer didn’t intend. We ended up becoming very close friends, 06:02.562 --> 06:07.834 and he became my first professional mentor for hacking. This was a career pivot. 06:07.834 --> 06:11.037 Instead of building things, she wanted to know how to break things. 06:11.704 --> 06:13.306 All this is happening in Canada, by the way. 06:13.306 --> 06:16.409 Tanya was living and working in the capital city of Ottawa. 06:16.876 --> 06:19.846 So, her new mentor was like, okay, so you want to be a hacker. 06:19.846 --> 06:21.147 I’ve got some work for you. 06:21.147 --> 06:23.883 You can help me do some penetration test. 06:23.883 --> 06:27.854 She’s like, okay, but I’m not exactly sure how. So, he told me 06:28.488 --> 06:31.657 on the Friday, okay, so, go learn Burp Suite this weekend. 06:31.758 --> 06:32.992 There’s videos on YouTube. 06:32.992 --> 06:33.793 Just go watch them. 06:33.793 --> 06:37.397 It’s not hard. [Music] So, she starts watching them. 06:37.430 --> 06:41.234 Burp Suite is a tool used to monitor the packets that go between your computer 06:41.534 --> 06:44.270 and an application or a network or a website 06:44.270 --> 06:46.973 so you can redirect all your computer’s traffic to it, 06:46.973 --> 06:48.808 and then Burp Suite will show you, hey, 06:48.808 --> 06:51.444 you went to this website and it responded with this code, 06:51.444 --> 06:51.677 and then 06:51.677 --> 06:55.348 your computer sent this information back, and then this website sent back a cookie 06:55.515 --> 06:57.083 which has this data in it. 06:57.083 --> 07:00.553 It’s kinda like getting under the hood of a car but for network traffic. 07:00.953 --> 07:04.457 Burp Suite is really cool; you can capture that data and replay it if you want. 07:04.624 --> 07:06.959 Like, maybe you look in the cookie that a website sent you, 07:06.959 --> 07:10.997 and it says that your user ID is 5000. So, 07:11.230 --> 07:16.402 what if you change that user ID to 5001 and then reconnect 07:16.402 --> 07:20.072 to the site and present this cookie which has a different user ID? 07:20.206 --> 07:23.209 Will it think that you are a different user? 07:23.643 --> 07:27.613 It’s kind of like a way to do surgery on the packets that your computer is sending 07:27.880 --> 07:31.551 to an application or website, and it’s possible to manipulate your packets 07:31.551 --> 07:35.087 enough to make the site do some very strange things. 07:35.721 --> 07:38.791 So, she comes back in on Monday with the basics of Burp Suite understood, 07:38.991 --> 07:40.359 and he tells her, okay, great. 07:40.359 --> 07:44.697 Spend a few hours a day trying to hack this website, and tell me what you find. 07:45.465 --> 07:49.535 He says… I’m gonna be observing you silently while you're working, 07:50.069 --> 07:53.072 and I just need you to report anything that you find. 07:53.072 --> 07:53.940 I was like, great. 07:53.940 --> 07:56.576 So, the first night I just found really tiny things, 07:56.576 --> 07:57.243 the second night 07:57.243 --> 07:59.245 I found really tiny things, and the third night 07:59.245 --> 08:01.814 he kinda gave me a lecture and he’s like, listen, Tanya, 08:01.814 --> 08:02.982 you've gotta find something. 08:02.982 --> 08:05.518 You can't do a pen test and not find something big. 08:05.518 --> 08:07.954 I need you to really think outside the box. 08:07.954 --> 08:09.655 Take off your developer hat. 08:09.655 --> 08:11.257 Put on your black hat. 08:11.257 --> 08:13.893 So, I just tried everything I could think 08:13.893 --> 08:16.863 of, and I found server-side request forgery. 08:16.863 --> 08:20.800 Now, I didn’t understand server-side request… How’d you find it? Basically, 08:20.800 --> 08:26.105 there was an e-mail field and I just started entering in code. 08:26.105 --> 08:30.109 I entered in an e-mail but then after, I just put in everything 08:30.109 --> 08:33.312 I could think of, like all sorts of code, all sorts of stuff. 08:33.312 --> 08:38.150 Inadvertently, I started copying and deleting files on the web server. 08:38.751 --> 08:43.256 [Music] Yeah, and I ended up crashing the production web server, 08:43.256 --> 08:46.259 and it turned out I had polluted the database as well. 08:46.292 --> 08:48.094 They had to restore both from backup. 08:48.094 --> 08:48.995 So, I called my boss. 08:48.995 --> 08:52.031 I’m like, I found something and I have crashed everything. 08:52.031 --> 08:53.132 He’s like, what? 08:53.132 --> 08:55.234 This is production. You can't crash production. 08:55.234 --> 08:59.438 I’m like, well, I found an exploit and you told me to prove 08:59.438 --> 09:03.609 that I had exploited it, so here’s — you know, I took the whole thing down. 09:03.609 --> 09:06.345 He’s just — he yelled at me and was really angry. 09:06.345 --> 09:07.880 He’s like, how did you do it? 09:07.880 --> 09:09.248 I’m like, these are all the commands I did. 09:09.248 --> 09:11.684 He’s like, well, this is garbage. This shouldn't do anything. 09:11.684 --> 09:14.487 I’m like, well, I guess it did, right? 09:14.487 --> 09:16.622 I was like, well, weren't you watching me the whole time? 09:16.622 --> 09:19.592 He’s like, no, that’s just something I said to make you feel better. 09:20.426 --> 09:21.193 I was like, well, 09:22.261 --> 09:23.529 what is the client gonna say? 09:23.529 --> 09:25.431 He’s like — I’m like, I could talk to them. 09:25.431 --> 09:27.333 He’s like, no, they don’t know that you're testing. 09:27.333 --> 09:30.503 I’m like, but you said I’m a subcontractor, right? 09:30.536 --> 09:34.640 So, the contract I signed with him that I was subcontracting that they knew. 09:34.974 --> 09:36.609 They had no idea I was on their network. 09:36.609 --> 09:40.880 So, he had given me the keys to production to some random client. 09:41.247 --> 09:42.515 They had no idea I was on there. 09:42.515 --> 09:44.850 I destroy everything, and he’s like, great, now 09:44.850 --> 09:47.386 I’m gonna get yelled at tomorrow and it’s all your fault. 09:47.386 --> 09:48.054 I’m like, really? 09:48.054 --> 09:52.825 This is all — he was really pissed at me. I think 09:52.825 --> 09:56.562 they both learned a lesson that day, but Tanya was hooked more than before. 09:56.562 --> 10:00.833 To copy and delete files on a web server all by putting in some code 10:00.833 --> 10:02.168 through a form field? 10:02.168 --> 10:04.704 Wow, such power. 10:04.704 --> 10:06.706 But wow, such weakness. 10:06.706 --> 10:11.577 These apps she was seeing are surprisingly weak, and she was drawn to that. 10:11.844 --> 10:14.747 What are other tricks and techniques for making an app 10:14.747 --> 10:18.417 give you data that it’s not supposed to do or do things it shouldn't let you do? 10:18.985 --> 10:22.521 She got more and more into security, wanting to get more hands-on 10:22.521 --> 10:27.293 with everything related to it. I kept annoying the security team constantly. 10:27.693 --> 10:29.261 I would report security incidents. 10:29.261 --> 10:31.230 I would fix all the security bugs. 10:31.230 --> 10:33.866 I kept asking if I could use security tools. 10:33.866 --> 10:37.069 I volunteered to work on their projects. 10:37.236 --> 10:40.439 One day, they said 10:40.439 --> 10:44.043 that I could sit in on an incident and just watch and shut up. 10:44.243 --> 10:47.079 Literally, I did not have a seat at the table. 10:47.079 --> 10:50.683 They had only so many seats that would actually fit at the table, 10:50.683 --> 10:53.152 so I was actually against the wall at the back of the room 10:53.152 --> 10:56.155 just being — zipping it, being quiet like they told me to. 10:56.622 --> 10:58.958 Then I remember them putting all of this stuff on the screen 11:00.092 --> 11:02.561 and looking at it and being like, oh, 11:02.561 --> 11:06.032 that’s SQL. Oh, that’s pretty bad. 11:06.632 --> 11:11.103 So, I said to them, I am seeing code here. 11:11.637 --> 11:13.172 We need to look at this. 11:13.172 --> 11:15.207 Can we talk? 11:15.207 --> 11:17.643 They're like, you can read that? 11:17.643 --> 11:18.544 Just because someone’s 11:18.544 --> 11:22.014 trying to SQL-inject you doesn't mean they're successful, right? 11:22.682 --> 11:25.284 But I’m like, someone’s attacking us. 11:25.284 --> 11:28.721 Every organization’s getting attacked all day, all the time, but the fact 11:28.721 --> 11:33.459 that I could sit there and read code — they were like, oh, she’s an asset. 11:34.026 --> 11:39.231 Then a few weeks later they said, oh, we’ve opened a job on the security team. 11:39.899 --> 11:41.200 I was like, oh my gosh, I’m gonna apply. 11:41.200 --> 11:43.436 They're like, obviously it’s for you, silly. 11:43.436 --> 11:47.907 So, they let me transfer onto the team, and I was just — I was so excited 11:47.907 --> 11:49.275 to be a part of their team. 11:49.275 --> 11:52.645 With this new position she proved herself again and again 11:52.645 --> 11:56.582 and rose up the ladder, eventually landing in a security leadership position 11:56.816 --> 11:59.819 at an organization which was within the Canadian government. 12:00.052 --> 12:05.091 She was in charge of making sure that agency and all its apps were secure. 12:05.091 --> 12:08.561 One day she came to work and had an e-mail waiting for her. [Music] 12:09.562 --> 12:11.797 I receive an e-mail from Vice Magazine 12:11.797 --> 12:14.834 and it says, dear Tanya, 12:16.035 --> 12:20.506 we know you work at this place and that you're the leader of this team. 12:20.840 --> 12:22.942 We would like a quote for you for our magazine 12:22.942 --> 12:27.513 about how your data is for sale on the dark web and how you feel about — 12:27.513 --> 12:31.851 that your data is worth only $48 Canadian dollars. 12:31.851 --> 12:33.452 Here’s a link if you want to see more. 12:33.452 --> 12:40.626 It’s a link to Pastebin, and on it it says, here’s a sample of the data 12:40.626 --> 12:45.397 from the name of my organization, and to get more, go here. 12:45.598 --> 12:49.001 Then I go there, and they're auctioning my data 12:49.301 --> 12:53.072 for the Bitcoin equivalent of approximately $48 Canadian dollars, 12:53.606 --> 12:58.744 which is not a lot of money. What a way to be notified that your agency 12:58.744 --> 13:01.914 has suffered a data breach, by getting an e-mail asking you for a quote 13:01.914 --> 13:06.051 on how you feel about your data being for sale. So, I talked to my team. 13:06.051 --> 13:06.352 I’m like, 13:08.354 --> 13:11.791 aah! All of us are just flabbergasted. 13:11.791 --> 13:13.459 We were like, first of all, what is this data? 13:13.459 --> 13:14.794 Is this actually our data? 13:14.794 --> 13:17.797 So, we're looking through all of our apps, and this is when I realized 13:18.330 --> 13:20.933 my app inventory was not complete. 13:20.933 --> 13:22.334 We were missing lots and lots of apps 13:22.334 --> 13:25.805 that I did not know about that I am supposed to be securing. So, I go — I find it — that data is in there. 13:46.559 --> 13:49.562 The Pastebin sample does look a little familiar. 13:49.562 --> 13:52.531 I’m like, oh no. 13:52.531 --> 13:55.534 So, I go and I talk to my boss, and my boss was so pissed. 13:55.901 --> 13:56.902 He was like — 13:58.070 --> 13:58.771 have you ever had 13:58.771 --> 14:01.774 someone say your name in a way where it sounds like a swear word? 14:01.974 --> 14:05.144 They were just like, Tanya! 14:06.111 --> 14:09.782 I am not really good when people are upset with me, and so, 14:09.782 --> 14:12.117 I was like, well, sir, I — you know, 14:12.117 --> 14:14.253 our data is for sale on the dark web; that’s true, 14:14.253 --> 14:17.156 but I think the bigger problem is that it’s only $48. 14:17.156 --> 14:19.525 Don’t you feel we're worth more than that? 14:19.525 --> 14:22.528 He was not impressed. 14:22.628 --> 14:26.332 Somehow my name was at a higher pitch the next time he said it, and he’s like, 14:26.498 --> 14:30.936 you are gonna go fix this now!
